Adult Rock flathead (Platycephalus laevigatus) typically attain a maximum total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a value that places them among the larger members of the Platycephalidae. This ultimate length is achieved through a growth trajectory that appears strongly influenced by the cool, temperate waters of their southern Australian distribution. In these environments, which average 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C], reproduction is timed to the austral spring and summer months. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches a peak value of 6% [GSI = 6%] during the spawning season at a water temperature of 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C].

Neonatal body mass in Rock flathead is exceptionally low, with newly emerged larvae weighing approximately 0.00038 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00038 grams]. This minute wet weight at birth corresponds to the small, pelagic eggs characteristic of the genus, which upon fertilisation drift in the water column. The onset of exogenous feeding follows a brief endotrophic phase; yolk-sac larvae begin their free-swimming existence after roughly 10 days [ab = roughly 10 days] when reared at 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C]. This rapid transition to active feeding is critical for survival in the planktonic environment, where first-feeding success directly governs early cohort mortality.

Sexual maturity in this species is attained at a total length of 26.4 centimeters [Lp = 26.4 centimeters]. Reaching this pubertal length typically requires several growing seasons, reflecting the relatively slow growth rates imposed by cool coastal waters. The length-based trigger for maturity ensures that individuals have accumulated sufficient somatic reserves before investing in reproductive effort. Field surveys indicate that most 26.4 centimeter fish are actively undergoing vitellogenesis or spermatogenesis, confirming that this size threshold reliably marks the onset of reproductive capability in both sexes across the species' temperate range.

The ultimate wet weight of Rock flathead reaches approximately 767 grams [Wwi = approximately 767 grams] in large, fully grown adults. This asymptotic mass is derived from the length-weight relationship characteristic of the species and corresponds to individuals that have achieved their maximum total length of 50 centimeters. Such heavy fish are typically encountered in deeper, structured habitats where prey resources are abundant and where they occupy an apex position within the demersal fish assemblage.

Longevity records for Rock flathead indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years] under the prevailing thermal regime of 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C]. This remarkable longevity is among the highest reported for platycephalid fishes and likely reflects a slow metabolic pace coupled with low natural mortality rates in the adult stage. The species' extended lifespan, when combined with its moderate fecundity and late onset of maturity at 26.4 centimeters, places it firmly within a slow life-history strategy. Such a strategy renders the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as the removal of large, old individuals can severely reduce the reproductive potential of the population.
